newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Drachma dilemma clouds Greek outlook.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Drachma dilemma clouds Greek outlook.

text.p: Greece's determination to earn a place in European Monetary Union membership in 2001 is prompting some investors to consider the country as the next potential hot spot for major yield convergence, analysts said on Friday.

But it won't all be plain sailing for the international visitor to the Greek bond market. Despite impressive progress, the Maastricht convergence criteria are far from fulfilled and high debt levels continue to be bothersome.
The biggest cloud on the horizon is a potential depreciation of the Greek drachma.

"Greece has surprised everyone with the progress they're making on EMU...but the biggest catch is the exchange rate -- they're going to have to let it depreciate," said Sara Zervos, emerging market strategist at BZW in London.
David Calver, analyst at Merrill Lynch in London, said Greece was still on track to join EMU, but added things could get turbulent for markets towards the end of the year.

"In the short term, six months, things should be fine but in the longer term, concerns Greece will have to devalue prior to entering the ERM could cause market volatility," he said. "But I still think it's good value."

If Greece is to join the European single currency -- and some analysts still regard that as highly unlikely -- the drachma should enter the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1999 to fulfil the requisite two year pre EMU membership.
"The market expects a devaluation to be required prior to ERM entry," said Calver. Hence the dilemma for Greek bonds.
"From a European investor's perspective, the yield enhancement does look good -- every bit of Greek policy is geared towards joining EMU," agreed Zervos.
"The only danger sign is that they have to enter the ERM and right now the drachma is a bit overvalued -- that's the risky scenario in the next six months," she said.

Greek 10-year debt currently yields nearly four percentage points more than comparable German Bunds. But while the long-term outlook is considered positive, none of the London-based analysts was prepared to make a concrete forecast for how much the spread may narrow.
Greece has made impressive strides on the Maastricht convergence criteria, but it still has a long way to go.

Inflation has fallen by around two percentage points so far this year to 5.4 percent and the deficit/GDP ratio is seen falling to around 5.5 percent by year end from 7.4 percent at the end of 1996 -- still a way off the 3.0 percent EMU criteria.

Analysts said things would get more uncomfortable for the bond market around October-November, when the central bank is expected to announce its foreign exchange policy for the following year, and 1998 budget preparations are in full swing.
Investors looking for a bargain will find they have already missed out on the best deals, said Calver.
"Interest rates have come down heavily this year so investments are not quite as attractive, and people are still worried about the drachma," he said.

With around one-third of the public deficit going in debt interest payments, the government has been keen to foster falling Greek interest rates. The 12-month T-bill rate is currently at 9.6 percent -- where analysts expect it to plateau for a while -- down from 11.5 percent at the end of last year.
That has left the central bank with the exchange rate as the only anti-inflation weapon at its disposal, resulting in its "hard drachma" policy to reduce the impact of imported inflation.
So if the currency is forced to devalue for ERM membership, not only will international investors' returns be eroded, but inflation will be in danger of accelerating.
But one trader at a Greek bank in London, was optimistic about the performance of the bond market in the coming year.
"With inflation falling and forecast to fall further this year and next, the bond market should pick up and we should see a decent rally between now and the middle of next year," he said.

"Whether it will be the next convergence play or not is up in the air...The initial big trade has probably passed by, but in an environment of ever shrinking returns, Greek bonds will soon start to look attractive."
